extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in philosophy of mathematics, logic, and foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative exposition of Brouwer's intuitionism and Hilbert's formalist programme, focusing on their standards for what counts as meaningful mathematics and the impact of Gödel’s incompleteness theorems. The piece explains each position's criteria for admissible mathematics and evaluates their defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness of mathematical claims (Brouwer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical reasoning should be guided by intuition: the subject matter of mathematics is human mental constructions, and claims about actual infinite sets are meaningless. 'The only meaningful portion' of mathematics is finitary mathematics; any theorising about uncountable sets is 'utterly meaningless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brouwer insists mathematics be grounded in the 'ur-intuition' (the intuition of the flow of time); mathematical truth consists in the human construction of a proof (or construction of a disproof). He denies 'non-experienced truths' in mathematics and treats mathematical objects as dependent on human thought in general rather than independently existing entities. This entails rejecting parts of classical mathematics that appeal to actual infinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of impredicative definitions (intuitionist constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impredicative definitions are unacceptable because they require that an object has been constructed before it can be constructed, yielding vicious circularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Brouwerian intuitionism, impredicative definitions violate the constructive requirement that objects must be built in temporal mental acts; thus any definition that quantifies over a totality including the thing being defined is ruled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-as-construction (intuitionist criterion for proof and truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth of any mathematical statement—or its negation—consists in human construction of its proof (or disproof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs should be constructive and often inductive; many classical inferential practices (e.g., reliance on non-constructive existence proofs) are rejected. Examples: inductive derivation of arithmetic laws from 'intuitive counting' and the main theorem of arithmetic via complete induction as a natural mathematical act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of potential but rejection of actual infinites (intuitionism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential infinites (e.g., the countable infinite supply of natural numbers) are permitted, but larger actual infinite sets (uncountable sets) are incomprehensible and meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although humans can grasp the idea of a continuum in terms of potential infinite divisibility, they cannot construct uncountable sets in any temporal process; therefore Cantorian set theory and claims about actual infinities must be abandoned under strict intuitionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness of mathematics must be finitary (Hilbert)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolutely all of the strictly meaningful parts of mathematics must be grounded in intuition; intuitions are finitary, so meaningful mathematics must be finitary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert holds that finitary mathematics provides the secure, meaningful core. However, unlike Brouwer, Hilbert endorses treating infinitary mathematics as 'ideal'—a formal, possibly meaningless, but useful extension—so long as the finitary core remains intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ideal (infinitary) elements only as useful fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal elements are 'strictly meaningless claims' but are accepted because they are useful and important to mathematics (e.g., imaginary unit i, points at infinity); their importance lies in usefulness rather than truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert treats infinitary additions as formal devices that complete theories and make mathematics more powerful; examples include imaginary numbers, transfinite numbers, and points at infinity in projective geometry. Their acceptance is instrumental: they must not undermine the meaningful finitary mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy condition for ideal extensions: consistency/conservativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension of a domain by the addition of ideal elements is legitimate only if the extension does not cause contradictions to appear in the old, narrower domain; the programme requires a proof of consistency (and conservativeness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's programme demanded finitary proofs that ideal-extended theories do not produce contradictions in finitary mathematics. In practice, this meant finitary mathematics should be able to prove the consistency of the richer (infinitary) theory; Gödel's second incompleteness theorem shows this is impossible for sufficiently strong systems, undermining Hilbert's original aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term-formalism and game-formalism blend (Hilbert's methodological criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert combines term-formalism (mathematics as meaningful statements about symbols) with game-formalism (mathematics as rule-governed manipulation of empty symbol strings) to account for both finitary content and infinitary formal theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term-formalism accounts for quasi-concrete syntactical objects and basic finitary mathematics; game-formalism provides a way to handle infinitary mathematics as formal games. Each faces problems alone (term-formalism struggles with reals, game-formalism is oversimplified), motivating Hilbert's synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumentalist constraints for accepting ideal mathematics (Paseau)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paseau lists instrumentalist constraints that the ideal parts of mathematics must deliver: Reliability, Consistency, Conservativeness, Avoidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert insisted on proofs of (2) consistency and (3) conservativeness. Paseau adopts 'reliability' as a focus: for all real p, if p is provable in real and ideal mathematics then p is true. Paseau argues that the instrumentalist argument need not be a formal proof; inductive evidence can suffice to warrant these constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of inductive evidence in place of formal proof (Paseau's instrumentalist defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrumentalists can rely on inductive evidence, enumerative evidence, or inference to the best explanation rather than a formal proof to justify reliability of ideal mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paseau argues that while a proof of reliability would be epistemically superior, inductive reasons can provide good justification for belief in the reliability of ideal mathematics. Objections that proofs give higher credence are acknowledged but do not defeat the inductive defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gödelian constraint on self-consistency proofs (meta-mathematical limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any consistent system F that can carry out elementary arithmetic, the consistency of F cannot be proven in F itself; the second incompleteness theorem therefore blocks Hilbert's requirement that finitary mathematics prove its own consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central technical obstacle to Hilbert’s programme: any formal system strong enough to express its own consistency cannot prove that consistency internally (unless it is inconsistent). This result is what led to the widespread view that Hilbert’s original project is 'dead' in its intended form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical desideratum: account should respect mathematical practice (Linnebo's constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: The task of the philosopher of mathematics is to account for mathematical practice as it actually is, not to revise it gratuitously; radical revisions require very good reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is used as a critique of Brouwer: completely revising mathematics to fit intuitionism conflicts with how mathematics is actually practiced, so intuitionists must justify such disruptive revision given the costs (abandoning much accepted mathematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Success condition for mathematical instrumentalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical instrumentalism's success condition is that 'the upper tier of mathematics—the instrument—be deemed successful from the perspective of the lower tier.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames success as the instrument (infinitary theory) producing outcomes valuable to the lower-tier (finitary) mathematics (e.g., yielding true finitary consequences). Success need not be established by formal proof; it can be established by the instrument delivering the desired epistemic or pragmatic outcomes.
